summaryHeading: A traffic ticket can affect a CDL driver differently
summary: Federal rules generally prohibit Texas courts from "masking" a CDL holder's conviction — no deferred disposition, no defensive driving dismissal — so a CDL ticket is either contested for dismissal or reduction, or it becomes a conviction on your record.
This applies even in your personal car: a speeding ticket in your pickup on the weekend counts against your CDL just like one in the truck.

Two "serious" violations (15+ mph over, following too closely, improper lane change, texting, and others) within three years bring a 60-day CDL disqualification under federal rules; a third brings 120 days. Employers and DAC reports see every conviction.

sections.heading: Why a CDL Ticket Is Different From Everyone Else's
paragraphs: When a regular driver gets a speeding ticket in El Paso, the court will often offer deferred disposition or a defensive driving course, and the ticket is dismissed without a conviction. Texas law itself excludes CDL holders from the driving safety course dismissal (Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45A.352 (formerly art. 45.0511)), and federal regulations go further: under the FMCSA's anti-masking rule (49 CFR 384.226, stated generally) a state may not defer, divert or otherwise keep a CDL holder's traffic conviction off the record. Texas courts apply this in municipal and JP court alike.

The practical result is close to binary. Either the ticket is dismissed on its merits or by negotiation, or you plead and it goes to DPS and into your federal CDLIS record. There is little middle ground, which is why CDL drivers who "just pay it" to save time are making the most expensive choice available.

We know which prosecutors will consider amending a charge to a non-moving violation and which judges want a clean motor vehicle record before they'll dismiss. This page is general information, not legal advice about your case.

sections.heading: Serious Violations and the 60/120-Day Disqualification
paragraphs: The federal CDL rules sort violations into tiers. Routine convictions — a few miles over the limit, an equipment ticket — add up on your DPS record and with your insurer but don't by themselves disqualify you. "Serious traffic violations" are different. Under 49 CFR 383.51, two of them within three years bring a 60-day disqualification of your CDL; three within three years bring 120 days.

sections.heading: Tickets in Your Personal Vehicle Still Count
paragraphs: The question we get most from CDL drivers is whether the Saturday speeding ticket in the family SUV matters. It does. Texas reports every conviction to DPS, and your license is a commercial license whether or not you were working at the time. Certain serious violations in a personal vehicle can also count toward the disqualification rule — and either way the conviction lands on the motor vehicle record your employer pulls each year.

Your employer sees more than the MVR. Carriers that subscribe to the DAC employment history report and FMCSA's Pre-Employment Screening Program see violations and inspection results, and some carriers terminate drivers after a set number of convictions regardless of circumstances. The time to call is before the appearance date, not after.
If you also hold a hazmat endorsement or drive for a company with a tight safety rating, mention it when you hire us — it changes how hard we push for a dismissal versus a reduced charge.

sections.heading: Building a CDL Case for Dismissal or an Amended Charge
paragraphs: When you hire us online or call 915-503-1600, we file a notice of appearance promptly. That stops any failure-to-appear warrant and routes everything to our office — important for drivers who are on the road in another state when the court date arrives.

Then we build the case. We pull the citation and the officer's notes; for speeding, the radar or lidar calibration records; for lane-change and following-too-close tickets, the dash camera and any crash report. Many CDL tickets have fixable problems — a wrong statute, an officer who has left the department, a speed measured on a grade where the device's tolerance matters. We present that to the prosecutor on the pretrial docket and ask for an outright dismissal. Where a dismissal isn't available, we work for an amendment to a non-moving violation such as defective equipment, which is reported differently and is not a serious violation under the federal rules. Our goal is to pursue the best available outcome based on the citation, driving record, court and circumstances.

Tickets from El Paso Police go to El Paso Municipal Court; tickets from a DPS trooper or deputy on I-10 go to a Justice of the Peace precinct; Anthony and Vinton write a steady stream of truck tickets on the west side. Each court has its own prosecutor and habits, and we appear in all of them.

sections.heading: Ports of Entry, the Zaragoza Bridge and Cross-Border Drivers
paragraphs: El Paso's trucking traffic is unlike any other Texas city's. Thousands of commercial vehicles cross daily at the Ysleta–Zaragoza port of entry and move along Zaragoza Road, Joe Battle Boulevard and the Border Highway to warehouses and transload yards. A driver pulling a drayage load from Juárez to an east-side yard can collect a citation in the two miles between the bridge and the dock.

Many of those drivers hold Mexican commercial licenses (Licencia Federal) rather than a Texas CDL, which raises its own questions about how a Texas conviction is reported and whether carrier status is affected. We handle those cases regularly. Se habla español. If you are dealing with a roadside inspection, overweight or logbook citation rather than a moving violation, see our trucking and DOT violations page — those tickets have a different structure and usually land in JP court. Not sure which court has your citation? Use the free ticket and warrant lookup.

faqs.q: Can a CDL holder take defensive driving to dismiss a ticket in Texas?
faqs.a: No. Texas excludes CDL holders from the driving safety course dismissal, and federal anti-masking rules generally prohibit the court from using deferred disposition or any other program to keep a CDL holder's conviction off the record. The ticket has to be dismissed or reduced on the merits, which is what we pursue.

faqs.q: Does a ticket in my personal vehicle affect my CDL?
faqs.a: Yes. Convictions in a personal vehicle are reported on your commercial license and show up on the motor vehicle record your employer pulls. Certain serious violations in a personal vehicle can also count toward a CDL disqualification.

faqs.q: What is a "serious traffic violation" for CDL purposes?
faqs.a: Under federal rules, these include speeding 15 mph or more over the limit, following too closely, improper lane changes, reckless driving, texting or hand-held phone use, and driving a commercial vehicle without a CDL or the proper endorsement. Two convictions in three years bring a 60-day disqualification; three bring 120 days.

faqs.q: Will my employer find out about the ticket?
faqs.a: If it becomes a conviction, very likely. Carriers pull motor vehicle records at least annually and many subscribe to DAC and PSP reports. A dismissed ticket does not appear as a conviction, which is why contesting the ticket is the realistic way to keep it from your employer.

faqs.q: I'm on the road out of state. Do I have to come back for court?
faqs.a: Generally not for a Class C ticket in El Paso County. We file an appearance and handle the pretrial docket for you. The only time you would need to be present is a trial, which is uncommon and something we'd plan with you around your schedule.

faqs.a: The same flat fee as any ticket: $59 in El Paso Municipal Court and $69 in JP, Horizon City, Socorro, San Elizario, Clint and Anthony courts. Multiple citations from the same stop are discounted add-ons.
